plot_cutoffs(cs01_ss, "OF", "thc", title = "Oral Fluid")











plot_cutoffs(cs01_ss, "BR", "thc", title = "Breath")











This is only THC
For five semi-random cutoffs
There are other compounds and other cutoffs to consider
Breath THC is measured in pg/pad (not ng/mL), so these cutoffs don’t separate anything for breath (the lines overlap). What cutoffs would make sense there?

title: 07-cs01-eda
text:
Possible Extensions
Our current question asks for a single compound…and you’ll need to decide that.
. . .
…but you could imagine a world where more than one compound or more than one matrix could be measured at the roadside.
. . .
So:


combination of the oral fluid and blood that would better predict recent use? (For example if an officer stopped a driver and got a high oral fluid, but could not get a blood sample for a couple of hours and got a relatively low result would this predict recent use better than blood (or OF) alone?
Is there a ratio of OF/blood that predicts recent use?
Machine learning model to determine optimal combination of measurements/cutoffs to detect recent use?


. . .
Things to keep in mind:

some matrices are easier to get at the roadside
time from use matters (trying to detect recent use)
we may not care equally about sensitivity and specificity

title: 09-written-communication
text:
Controlling code chunk output

Specified at the top of the chunk, one per line, with #|

```{r}
#| label: chunk-label
#| results: hide
#| fig-height: 4

```


eval: whether to execute the code chunk
echo: whether to include the code in the output
include: false: run the code, but show nothing (code or output) in the rendered document. Great for setup chunks (e.g., loading packages)
warning, message, and error: whether to show warnings, messages, or errors in the rendered document
fig-width and fig-height: control the width/height of plots
fig-cap: add a caption to a figure




Controlling for the whole document (in the YAML):

---
title: "Document Title"
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

title: 09-written-communication
section: Inline code: numbers in your text
text:
Inline code: numbers in your text
Typing numbers into your text by hand means they go stale (or are just wrong!) when your data or analysis changes.
Instead, compute them with inline code:
The mtcars dataset includes `r nrow(mtcars)` cars, with an average fuel efficiency of `r round(mean(mtcars$mpg), 1)` mpg.

…which renders as:

The mtcars dataset includes 32 cars, with an average fuel efficiency of 20.1 mpg.



The numbers in your conclusions are always the numbers from your analysis.

What does this mean?

Simply: You do the work so they don’t have to.

…also the aesthetic-usability effect exists: people perceive polished, attractive work as easier to use (and are more forgiving of its flaws).

Considerations

Platform: written? oral?

Setting: informal? formal?

Audience: technical? general?

title: 09-written-communication
text:
Choose informative titles
In written reports: Balance b/w short and informative (goal: concise)
. . .

Avoid: “Analyzing NHANES”

Better: “Data from the NHANES study shows that diet is related to overall health”
. . .
On visualizations: emphasize the take-home! (what’s learned or what action to take)
. . .

Avoid: “Boxplot of gender”

Better: “Twice as many females as males included for analysis”
. . .

Avoid: “Tickets vs. Time”

Better: “Staff unable to respond to incoming tickets; need to hire 2 FTEs”

title: 09-written-communication
text:
Benefits of written communication
Your audience has time to process…but the explanation has to be there!
. . .
Visually: more on a single visualization
. . .
Yes, often there are different visualizations for reports/papers than for presentations/lectures.

title: 09-written-communication
text:
Data Science Reports in .qmd


As concise as possible
Important information introduced before referenced (datasets, jargon, etc.)
Necessary details (for your audience); nothing more

Be sure that the rendered output contains what you intended (plots displayed; headers etc.)
…and does NOT display stuff that doesn’t need to be there (messages/warnings suppressed, brainstorming, etc.)

Typical Sections: Introduction/Background, Setup, Data, Analysis, Conclusion, References

title: 09-written-communication
text:
Sharing your HTML

Self-contained output: everything (plots, CSS, JS) packed into a single .html file

---
title: "Document Title"
format:
  html:
    embed-resources: true
---
. . .

Without this, your plots/styling live in a separate _files/ folder…and break if the .html is shared/submitted on its own
Trade-off: larger file size

. . .






Warning



GitHub does not render .html files. Clicking your report on GitHub shows the source code. That’s expected! It doesn’t mean your render failed. Download the file and open it in a browser to check it.

title: 09-written-communication
text:
Controlling code chunk output

Specified at the top of the chunk, one per line, with #|

```{r}
#| label: chunk-label
#| results: hide
#| fig-height: 4

```
. . .

eval: whether to execute the code chunk
echo: whether to include the code in the output
include: false: run the code, but show nothing (code or output) in the rendered document. Great for setup chunks (e.g., loading packages)
warning, message, and error: whether to show warnings, messages, or errors in the rendered document
fig-width and fig-height: control the width/height of plots
fig-cap: add a caption to a figure

. . .

Controlling for the whole document (in the YAML):

---
title: "Document Title"
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

title: 09-written-communication
section: Inline code: numbers in your text
text:
Inline code: numbers in your text
Typing numbers into your text by hand means they go stale (or are just wrong!) when your data or analysis changes.
Instead, compute them with inline code:
The mtcars dataset includes `r nrow(mtcars)` cars, with an average fuel efficiency of `r round(mean(mtcars$mpg), 1)` mpg.
. . .
…which renders as:

The mtcars dataset includes 32 cars, with an average fuel efficiency of 20.1 mpg.

. . .
The numbers in your conclusions are always the numbers from your analysis.

title: 09-written-communication
text:
Editing & Proofreading

Did you end up telling a story?

Things missing?
Things to delete?


. . .

Do not fall in love with your words/code/plots

. . .

Do spell check
Do read it over before sending/presenting/submitting

title: 09-written-communication
text:
Aside: Citing Sources
When are citations needed?
. . .


“We will be doing our analysis using two different data sets created by two different groups: Donohue and Mustard + Lott, or simply Lott”


. . .


“Right to Carry Laws refer to laws that specify how citizens are allowed to carry concealed handguns when they’re away from home without a permit”


. . .


“In this case study, we are examining the relationship between unemployment rate, poverty rate, police staffing, and violent crime rate.”


. . .


“In the United States, the second amendment permits the right to bear arms, and this law has not been changed since its creation in 1791.”


. . .


“The Right to Carry Laws (RTC) is defined as”a law that specifies if and how citizens are allowed to have a firearm on their person or nearby in public.””


. . .
Reminder: You do NOT get docked points for citing others’ work. You can be at risk of an Academic Integrity violation if you don’t. When in doubt, give credit.

Note: .bib files can be included with BibTeX references using the bibliography parameter in your YAML

Part 2: Citations

Exercise 3
Find at least one fact on the Internet related to our CS01 main question (ideally, a source/fact we didn’t discuss in class already). Specify the fact here, including a citation to the original source.
This can use footnotes as discussed in class or some other approach to citation…so long as we have the information an its original source.


Exercise 4
The following paragraph has been included in your lab…but it’s missing citations. Bold the sentences that you feel need citation. (You don’t have to add in the citations. Just determine that a citation is necessary.)

In America, almost two-thirds of US trauma center admissions are the result of motor vehicle accidents (MVAs). Among these accidents, 60% result from drivers who test positive for a drug, and the most commonly-detected substances are alcohol and cannabis. Despite being federally illegal, cannabis use in America has increased steadily over the last 20 years, much of which has been attributed to its use being decriminalized and/or legal at the state level. Given its rise in popularity and the rate at which it shows up in toxicology reports completed at the roadside after accidents, public health concerns arise as to its safety while driving. Some states have recently begun to set limits for marijuana usage. Here, using a double-blinded randomized control trial, we identify a plausible biomarker for detection of recent marijuana usage for potential use at the roadside to determine if an individual has driven under the influence of cannabis.



Exercise 5
Determine two changes you would make to the above paragraph to improve its effectiveness (clarity, conciseness, etc.). Would you remove information? Add? Reorder? Change to include specifics? Etc. Feel free to state the changes, without actually making the edits.
